structure.title: The Visit at Dawn · A visitor before daylight
structure.text: Crito arrives able to arrange an escape and bearing news about the ship whose return sets the date of Socrates' death. Time, money and willing helpers all favour action. Socrates asks his friend to put each advantage aside long enough to consider whether the action is just.

structure.title: The Plea and the Argument · The friends reckon with a lifetime of arguments
structure.text: Crito fears disgrace for abandoning a friend and grief for the children left behind. Socrates makes their earlier agreement against doing wrong the starting point, including the uncomfortable case in which somebody has already wronged you.

structure.title: The Laws of Athens Speak · Imagine Athens asking the questions
structure.text: Socrates lends the Laws a voice. They appeal to upbringing, benefits received and the decision to remain in Athens. An escape that seemed a private transaction between friends now has an imagined third party demanding a hearing.

people.name: Crito
people.role: The friend with the means to help
people.text: He has considered the bribes and the danger to accomplices. The care already invested in his plan explains why Socrates' refusal to start from its practical advantages is such a difficult thing to hear.

people.name: The Laws
people.text: They speak as parents and as parties to an agreement. Those claims depend on different kinds of obligation, even though Socrates gives them a single voice.

context.title: The city has just condemned him
context.text: The immediate question concerns the justice of a particular escape after a trial. Socrates and Crito must decide how the wrongfulness of a verdict bears on the wrongfulness of a proposed response.

notice.why: Crito repeatedly hears what people will say after his friend's death. Socrates asks whether a crowd has any more authority here than spectators have over the training of an athlete.

notice.text: Notice when residence starts to sound like consent.
notice.why: The Laws point to years Socrates could have spent elsewhere. Whether staying put gives them everything they claim depends on what a citizen could reasonably understand that choice to mean.

opening: The escape has been arranged. Money is available, friends will help, and Socrates can leave prison before his execution. Crito cannot understand why he hesitates: staying will abandon his children and make his friends look cowardly. Socrates insists that a wrongful sentence does not settle whether escaping would be right. In a conversation with almost no room left for abstraction, Plato makes a man account for his obligations to the city that has condemned him, while someone who loves him begs him to live.
